questions.text: What is the general purpose of an admixture in the checked BCI source?

options.text: To alter properties of the concrete mix or hardened product
To classify stone by geological origin
To join copper tubing only by solder
To replace all aggregate with aluminum

questions.rationale: BCI states that admixtures may be added to a concrete mix to alter its properties or those of the hardened product.

questions.text: Which admixture function best describes an accelerator?

options.text: It hastens setting and strength development
It delays setting to keep concrete plastic longer
It forms a patina on copper
It cuts stone into flagstone

questions.rationale: Salvan and BCI describe accelerators as materials that speed up or hasten setting and early strength development.
questions.explanation: 10—20% is excessive and would significantly reduce strength. 0.5—1% is insufficient for freeze-thaw protection (incidental air, not intentional entrainment). 20—30% would be foam, not properly entrained air. Air entrainment typically produces 2—8% air by volume, with bubble diameter 10—1000 micrometers. This is the standard range for freeze-thaw protection. Air entrainment = 2—8% volume. Each 1% air reduces compressive strength ~3—5%. Trade-off: durability vs. strength.

questions.text: Which admixture function best describes a retarder?

options.text: It delays or extends the setting time of cement paste
It increases galvanic action between metals
It turns rubble into ashlar
It removes all water from concrete before placement

questions.rationale: Salvan describes retarders as materials that delay or extend setting time, especially useful when heat accelerates hydration.
questions.code_citation: ASTM C494 dosage guidelines; concrete admixture best practices

questions.text: Why may retarders be useful in hot-weather concrete placement according to Salvan?

options.text: Heat accelerates hydration, reducing time for placing, consolidating, and finishing
Heat turns concrete into non-ferrous metal
Heat eliminates the need for workability
Heat makes all aggregates unsuitable

questions.rationale: Salvan explains that hot weather accelerates hydration and reduces available placing, consolidating, and finishing time.
questions.explanation: Accelerating would worsen hot-weather placement (opposite of goal). Type B specifically affects set time; no effect is not an option for this admixture. Reversing set time is impossible. Type B retarders delay set time by 1—6 hours, extending workability and preventing premature stiffening in hot conditions. Type B = retardation (delay). For hot weather. Not recommended for cold weather (would slow strength gain).

questions.text: What is the source-checked effect of air-entraining agents?

options.text: They disperse microscopic air bubbles and can improve workability and freeze-thaw resistance
They cut stone into dimension slabs
They weld steel beams together
They make concrete contain no cement paste

questions.rationale: BCI describes air-entraining agents as dispersing microscopic air bubbles to improve workability and freeze-thaw or scaling resistance.
questions.explanation: Accelerating in hot weather (where hydration is already fast) is unnecessary and can cause thermal stress. Slowing is contrary to acceleration purpose. Type C is not appropriate for all weather; it's specifically for cold conditions. Type C accelerators speed hydration, developing high 1-day strength. Used in cold weather to compensate for slow natural hydration at low temperatures. Type C = acceleration. For cold weather. Not recommended for hot weather (would increase thermal cracking risk).

questions.text: Water-reducing agents or superplasticizers are used to:

options.text: Reduce mixing water needed for desired workability
Increase water without limit
Create a copper-zinc alloy
Classify marble as igneous

questions.rationale: BCI describes water-reducing agents or superplasticizers as reducing the amount of mixing water needed for desired workability.
questions.explanation: Admixtures do affect strength indirectly through water-cement ratio modification. Water reduction increases strength (lower w/c), not decreases it. Doubling strength from 10% water reduction is unrealistic; typical gain is 5—15%. Reducing water by 10% (w/c = 0.50 → ~0.45) increases strength approximately 5—15%. The exact increase depends on cement type and curing. 30 MPa × 1.08 ≈ 32 MPa (conservative estimate). Water reduction ≈ strength increase. Lower w/c = higher strength (approximately 10 MPa increase per 0.05 reduction in w/c for normal Portland cement).
questions.code_citation: Concrete strength vs. w/c relationship; ASTM C494 effects

questions.text: Why can reducing water while maintaining workability increase strength?

options.text: Lower water-cement ratio generally increases strength
More voids always increase strength
Extra bleed water strengthens the paste
Strength depends only on stone color

questions.rationale: BCI states lowering the water-cement ratio generally results in increased strength.
questions.explanation: Standard reducers (Type A) only reduce 5—10%. Accelerators don't reduce water demand; Types F/G do. Air-entraining agents (C260) are different from C494 admixtures; minimal water reduction. Types F and G are superplasticizers providing 15—30% water reduction (compared to 5—10% for standard Type A reducers). They enable self-consolidating concrete and very low water-cement ratios. Type F/G = superplasticizers = high-range water reduction (15—30%). Use for SCC, flowing concrete, high strength.

questions.text: What does Salvan warn excess water can do in concrete?

options.text: Bleed, leave voids, decrease strength, increase permeability, and weaken paste
Create an anodized oxide layer
Change brass into bronze
Make welding unnecessary

questions.rationale: Salvan explains that excess water can bleed, evaporate to leave voids, decrease strength, increase permeability, and weaken cement paste.
questions.explanation: Type E combines water reduction + acceleration (cold-weather). Air entrainment is ASTM C260, not C494 admixtures. Superplasticizing is Types F and G, not Type D. Type D = Type A (water reduction) + Type B (retardation). Used in hot weather to achieve strength gain (water reduction benefit) while extending workability (retardation benefit). Type D = D for hot-weather (water reduction + retardation). Remember: D = (A) + (B).

questions.text: Surface-active agents or surfactants primarily reduce:

options.text: Surface tension of the mixing water
The number of stone courses
The carbon content of steel
The diameter of copper wire

questions.rationale: BCI states that surface-active agents reduce the surface tension of mixing water.
questions.explanation: Increasing water is not the purpose of water reducers. Type A affects water, so slump is not maintained constant without adjustment. Water cannot be eliminated; admixtures reduce, not eliminate, water demand. Type A water reducers reduce water demand by 5—10% for the same slump, allowing higher strength (lower water-cement ratio) or lower cement content (cost savings). Type A = water reduction only. No effect on set time (primary advantage over Types D, E, F, G which include other effects).

questions.text: Which answer stays inside the Batch 083 admixture source scope?

options.text: Match admixture category to source-checked function
Apply an external type-letter table not found in the checked sources
Invent a dosage limit
Assume every accelerator is always allowed in every concrete

questions.rationale: The repaired cluster is constrained to source-checked admixture categories and functions.
questions.explanation: Type A alone provides no retardation; set time would be normal or fast (not extended working time). Type C (acceleration) is counter-productive in hot weather; it would shorten working time, opposite of goal. Type F provides flowing concrete but doesn't specifically address hot-weather retardation; Type D is more targeted. Type D is optimized for hot weather with competing needs: strength gain (Type A water reduction) and extended working time (Type B retardation). In 32°C tropical temperature with complex column geometry, Type D prevents premature stiffening while improving strength. Hot weather + extended workability + strength = Type D. Hot weather + rapid strength = Type C (cold weather). Always match admixture type to project conditions.
questions.code_citation: ASTM C494 admixture selection; ACI 305.1 hot-weather concreting
